🌲 RaggieSoft Story Crossroads • Colville National Forest, June 2000

Five Miles Past the Back Fence, Nobody Screams—and Nobody Splits Them Up.

All their lives, eighteen-year-old triplets Luke, Tessa, and Sadie Bridger loved doing everything together—and all their lives, their parents yelled at them to spread their wings and go separate ways. Thrown out on their eighteenth birthday for refusing to separate, they step through the back barbed-wire fence into a million volcano-free acres of Northeast Washington forest with three canvas packs, a dome tent, Grandpa Owen’s tool roll, and his 1974 acoustic guitar.

Six Hands, One Unbreakable Rule

Meet Luke, Tessa, and Sadie Bridger

Fraternal brother Luke and his identical twin sisters Tessa and Sadie turn a single blissful night away from shouting into a hand-built life in the deep woods.

Born June 20, 1982 (Age 18 in Summer 2000)

Luke Bridger

Fraternal Triplet Brother • First-Person ("I") Narrator & Timber Framer

Steady, observant, and fiercely protective of his sisters, Luke learned traditional timber framing and dry-stone masonry spending summers in Grandpa Owen’s workshop. When their parents demanded the three triplets scatter onto separate lives at eighteen, Luke stepped up to hold the barbed wire open into the forest instead.

Musical Voice: Warm baritone-tenor harmony anchor and steady open-tuning rhythm guitar.

Born June 20, 1982 (Age 18 in Summer 2000)

Tessa Bridger

Identical Twin Sister #1 • Trail Mechanic, Forager & Hearth-Keeper

Direct, fearless, and happiest when solving a physical problem with her hands, Tessa turns anxiety into immediate motion. Give her an armful of willow switches, a pile of river stones, or a hillside of ripening huckleberries, and camp feels like a home before sundown.

Musical Voice: Clear, earthy alto-mezzo twin harmony and percussive acoustic rhythm.

Born June 20, 1982 (Age 18 in Summer 2000)

Sadie Bridger

Identical Twin Sister #2 • Navigator, Camp Medic & Songwriter

Thoughtful and steel-spined beneath a quiet smile, Sadie sees terrain patterns and seasonal weather shifts three moves ahead. Every evening by the keyhole fire, her thumb-picked 1970s acoustic chords turn three tired eighteen-year-olds into a band.

Musical Voice: Crystalline 1970s-style soprano-mezzo lead vocal, fingerstyle acoustic guitar, and three-part harmony arranger.

First Story Crossroads • Pure Wilderness, Zero Towns

Four Days of Oats Left: Where Do You Stake Their Claim?

At the end of Chapter 2, Luke, Tessa, and Sadie have scouted three completely different natural footholds inside the Cedar Run basin—each with its own shelter materials, wild food harvest, and sound when mountain rain begins to fall.

Option 1 • Creek-Bottom Terrace

The Creek-Bend Cedar Bench

Terrain: Twenty feet above three linked emerald pools of Cedar Run Creek

Shelter Plan: Use an eighty-foot wind-toppled western red cedar giant as a solid north back wall, splitting straight planks and roof shakes with Grandpa Owen’s froe for a raised timber cabin.

Wild Food & Water: Woven red-osier willow funnel traps for pan-sized cutthroat trout, wild strawberries, thimbleberries, and boiled young nettle and fireweed greens.

When It Rains: Rainwater patters across hand-split red-cedar shakes overhead while mist curls off the deep green pools twenty paces below the porch.

Follow This Route in Book Reader →
Option 2 • Sunny South Slope

The South-Facing Granite Overhang

Terrain: Half a mile upslope above five rolling acres of sunlit meadow

Shelter Plan: Enclose a bone-dry, twelve-foot-deep bedrock cliff alcove with dry-stacked granite slabs, peeled lodgepole poles, and moss-clay chinking beneath a natural vertical rock chimney flue.

Wild Food & Water: Gallons of sweet purple mountain huckleberries sun-dried on hot granite tables, crisp white wild-onion bulbs, and a cobble-lined cold spring seep sixty steps east.

When It Rains: A silver curtain of rain falls just past the dry stone overhang lip into the berry meadow while ten thousand tons of sun-warmed granite radiate stored heat behind your back.

Follow This Route in Book Reader →
Option 3 • High Tamarack Saddle

The Forgotten Stone Springhouse

Terrain: Wind-sheltered Douglas fir and tamarack saddle at the upper springhead

Shelter Plan: Hoist a sixteen-foot seasoned Douglas fir ridgepole, peeled tamarack rafters, and overlapping four-foot cedar-bark shingles atop four intact 1930s dry-stone walls.

Wild Food & Water: Apricot-scented Pacific golden chanterelles from damp fir duff, wild red raspberries, lemony wood sorrel, and a 42-degree indoor stone spring trough that chills food naturally.

When It Rains: Steady mountain rain whispers across thick cedar-bark shingles overhead while the crystal indoor spring trickles musically along the northern slate wall.

Hand-Built Homestead Progression

From a Two-Person Nylon Tent to Cedar & Stone

Step through all four stages to see how fallen western red cedar, Kettle Range granite, and creek clay become a dry, warm refuge.

Days 1–2 • Late June 2000

Two-Person Dome Tent, Keyhole Fire & Nine Hours of Unbroken Peace

Five miles past the washed-out logging culvert, Luke, Tessa, and Sadie pitch their weathered blue-and-white nylon tent on dry russet pine duff twenty paces above Cedar Run, unzipping both sleeping bags into one shared quilt for the quietest night of their lives.

Gathered & Hand-Worked Materials

  • Weathered blue-and-white fiberglass-pole dome tent
  • Dry wrist-thick lower ponderosa branches & shredded cedar inner-bark tinder
  • Keyhole stone fire ring dug down to bare mineral sand

Rain & Night Comfort: Protected beneath a hundred-foot ponderosa canopy, with three sharp stars visible through the roof mesh vent and zero shouting anywhere in the dark.

Week 1 • Late June 2000

Getting Off the Cold Ground With Windfall Cedar & Peeled Fir

Without felling a single live tree, the triplets buck seasoned corner blocks and split laser-straight red heartwood planks using Grandpa Owen’s steel froe and a hand-carved tamarack maul—lifting their sleeping deck eighteen inches clear of damp soil.

Gathered & Hand-Worked Materials

  • 80-foot wind-toppled western red cedar heartwood
  • Peeled Douglas fir floor stringers & forked ridgepole uprights
  • Spruce-root & cedar-bark lashings preserving their nylon cord

Rain & Night Comfort: When summer rain sweeps down the Kettle Range, water runs harmlessly beneath the elevated cedar floorboards while the U-shaped stone hearth bounces heat inward.

Weeks 2–6 • July–August 2000

Weatherproof Walls, Natural Chimney Draft & The Rain-Listening Porch

Week by week, the shelter expands: overlapping split-cedar shakes and four-foot bark shingles overhead, dry-stacked granite wind-walls chinked tight with creek clay and moss, and wide front eaves where all three sit dry with Grandpa’s guitar during afternoon downpours.

Gathered & Hand-Worked Materials

  • Two-on-one dry-stacked Kettle Range granite slabs
  • Creek-seep gray clay kneaded with moss and pine needles for draft-proof chinking
  • Overlapping split-cedar roof shakes weighted with binder poles

Rain & Night Comfort: Steady Pacific Northwest rain drumming against thick cedar shakes creates a warm, rhythmic hush inside—turning rainy afternoons into the triplets’ favorite hours of the week.

September–Winter 2000

Sun-Dried Berries, Cold-Spring Storage & Quiet Mountain Snowfalls

In Cedar Run’s sheltered 1,900-foot valley bench, golden October tamaracks give way to mild, misty late-autumn rains and occasional hushed winter snowfalls—met with stacked dry tamarack cordwood, smoked trout, dried huckleberries, and radiant stone hearths.

Gathered & Hand-Worked Materials

  • 42-degree bubbling stone spring trough & slate-lined root cache
  • Seasoned tamarack and Douglas fir cordwood stacked dry under extended eaves
  • Sun-dried huckleberry leather, wild onion braids, and woven cedar-bough door curtains

Rain & Night Comfort: When rain clears out at midnight—or six inches of quiet powder dusts the cedar boughs—the three wrap in wool blankets on the dry porch beneath a blazing horizon-to-horizon Milky Way.

Soothing Rain & Star-Filled Canopy

White Noise on Cedar Shakes—and the Milky Way Overhead

Tucked inside a sheltered 1,900-foot river-bench valley of Colville National Forest—hundreds of miles away from the Cascade volcanoes—Cedar Run enjoys long golden summers, gentle mountain rains, and mild winters graced by occasional quiet snowfalls that hush the pines without burying the valley.

After eighteen years in a loud, tense house, the triplets love the rain: standing in warm summer showers splashing off their faces, or curling up dry together listening to the steady white noise of rainwater pattering on their roof. And when the clouds part after midnight—eighty miles from city glare—the Milky Way blazes bright enough between the ponderosa crowns to shimmer across the dark creek pools.

1970s Acoustic Singer-Songwriter Warmth

The Cedar Run Campfire Songbook

Inspired by the warm 1975 era of fingerpicked acoustic guitars, upright parlor pianos, and three-part harmonies—played on Grandpa Owen’s 1974 Clearwater guitar.

Episode 1, Chapter 1 • Snowmelt and Red Cedar

Track 01: Cedar Run

Musical Feel: 1975 Pastoral Mountain Folk-Rock Ballad • Warm Analog Tape

Arrangement: Fingerpicked 6-string & shimmering 12-string acoustic guitars, rolling upright parlor piano, fretless bass, brushed snare, three-part sibling harmonies

Written after their very first silent night beyond the barbed-wire fence and their morning dip in the snowmelt granite pool—celebrating the nameless stream where nobody can split the three of them apart.
